business_problem: Drug development is long, resource-intensive, and uncertain, and Sanofi needed a better way to assess safety, efficacy, and competitive differentiation of drug candidates before advancing them into later clinical phases.
solution_summary: Sanofi describes an in-house AI-based digital twinning approach for early drug development using virtual patient populations. The implementation starts by ingesting available clinical trial data from live patients together with disease biology, pathophysiology, and known pharmacology data. These inputs are combined in a single computational framework built with quantitative systems pharmacology (QSP) modeling and AI models. Within that framework, Sanofi generates digital twins of human patients, simulates an investigational compound's mechanism of action on disease pathways, and measures predicted effects on clinical endpoints such as cytokines, lung function, and exacerbations. The virtual patient computer platform is then used to run blind predictions against Phase 1b trial results, compare candidate performance with existing therapies, and support R&D teams in deciding whether to move compounds into the next clinical phase.
data_flow: Sanofi combines clinical trial data from live patients with disease biology, pathophysiology, and known pharmacology in a single QSP-based computational framework. That framework generates virtual patients, simulates a compound's mechanism of action on disease pathways, and produces predicted clinical effects that R&D teams compare with observed Phase 1b results and other therapies before advancing development.
integration_points: Clinical trial data from live patients
business_outcome: Sanofi says virtual patients enable faster first assessments of safety and efficacy, better accuracy, potential reductions in the number of trial patients needed, evidence generation for hard-to-recruit subtypes, and research cycles that can shrink from weeks to hours.
metrics: 90% failure rate of new drug candidates during clinical development

architecture_clues: A single computational framework integrates disease biology, pathophysiology, known pharmacology, and live-patient clinical trial data.
Sanofi uses quantitative systems pharmacology (QSP) disease modeling to build digital twins and virtual patient populations.
The asthma implementation modeled relevant cell types and proteins to provide a multi-scale disease view.
Sanofi validated the model with a blind prediction against a Phase 1b proof-of-mechanism trial.
Virtual patient populations have already been built for multiple therapeutic indications.
